title: Providence (CCC 302–308)
hookLine: God guides creation, and invites us to cooperate

lines: THE BIRDS NEITHER SOW NOR REAP.
cards: "Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns: and your heavenly Father feedeth them." Jesus says it on a hillside, in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims.
It's a lovely line. It also raises a fair question from anyone with a job and a rent payment due on the first. So should we stop sowing?
Today's word is the Catechism's way of fitting God's care and our work together: providence.

teach.b: Day three hundred sixty-six met providence in Joseph's story; today, the Catechism's account. It starts somewhere surprising. Creation wasn't made finished.
It was made on a journey, heading toward a fullness it hasn't reached yet, and providence is the name for the ways God guides it along that road.
Scripture, the Catechism says, shows that care as concrete and close, reaching the smallest things.
That's why Jesus asks for a child's kind of trust: "Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you." Then the turn.
In the Catholic picture, God isn't a puppeteer.
He gives his creatures not only existence but the dignity of acting on their own, of being real causes for each other.
And to human beings he gives the power to share in providence freely: to tend the earth, to work, to look after one another.
Writing about himself and the others who labored with him in Corinth, Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims, "we are God's coadjutors." Helpers, fellow workers.

The Catechism takes up that phrase for people more broadly: through their actions, their prayers, and even their sufferings, people can enter freely into God's plan, and so become God's fellow workers.
So, back to the birds. They don't sow. People do, and on this reading, the sowing itself can be part of how God provides.
Providence isn't a reason to sit still, and it isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's trust that God is at work, and an invitation to work alongside.

how: Catholics speak of trusting in divine providence, and pair that trust with work; some pray before a task or a decision and offer the day's work to God in a morning prayer.

games.q: rent is due, and you've just heard the line about the birds who neither sow nor reap. what does the Catechism's reading point to?
o: work, and trust God in the work
worry, since it all depends on you
games.why: the Catechism says God invites people to share in providence through their actions, prayers and sufferings, as God's fellow workers.

practice: Pick one thing you're carrying this week, a bill, a test result, a hard conversation, and ask two questions: what part of this is mine to do, and what part is out of my hands?
Name your part, one step, nothing more, and let the other part go for now. If you pray, hand that part to God in your own words; if you don't, practice setting it down for these few minutes.

wordCard.voice: Providence. God's guidance of a creation still on its way, and the invitation to share in that work freely. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: providence. The word in Wisdom 14:3 for the Father's providence.

carryVoice: Your line: we are co-workers. Care from above, and hands at work down here. I'll be here tomorrow.
